related_questions.snippet: Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis (CRP), also known as Gougerot-Carteaud syndrome, is caused by disordered keratinization. It presents with asymptomatic hyperpigmented papules that can coalesce into plaques and are typically located on the upper trunk and neck of teens and young adults.

related_questions.question: Does CARP skin condition go away?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, Confluent and Reticulated Papillomatosis (CARP) (also known as CARP) can be treated and often goes away with appropriate therapy. While spontaneous resolution is possible, it's not the norm, and treatment is generally recommended to clear the skin condition.
snippet_highlighted_words: Yes, Confluent and Reticulated Papillomatosis (CARP) (also known as CARP) can be treated and often goes away with appropriate therapy

list.title: Treatment is effective:
list.snippet: CARP responds well to various treatments, including oral antibiotics like minocycline or doxycycline, and sometimes macrolide antibiotics like azithromycin.

list.title: Topical treatments:
list.snippet: Topical retinoids, antifungals, and other creams can also be used, either alone or in combination with oral medications.

list.title: Recurrence is possible:
list.snippet: While treatment can clear the skin, CARP can sometimes recur after stopping medication, especially if non-antibacterial treatments were used.

list.title: Spontaneous resolution:
list.snippet: In some cases, CARP may resolve on its own, but this can take months or even years.

list.title: Longer courses may be needed:
list.snippet: Some individuals may require longer courses of antibiotics or a combination of therapies to achieve lasting remission.

related_questions.question: What is the cause of CARP skin disease?
related_questions.snippet: It was thought to be caused by Malassezia furfur as CARP clinically resembles tinea versicolor. Still, studies have not been consistent with the detection of yeasts in patients with CARP. The current infectious theory is that CARP is caused by the bacteria, Dietzia papillomatosis.

text_blocks.snippet: Gougerot-Carteaud syndrome, also known as confluent and reticulated papillomatosis (CARP), is a rare skin condition characterized by small, scaly, brownish papules that can merge to form larger patches or plaques with a net-like (reticulated) pattern, according to the American Osteopathic College of Dermatology. It primarily affects the trunk, neck, and upper arms. The exact cause is unknown, but it's thought to be related to abnormal keratinization and may involve a fungal or bacterial component.
snippet_highlighted_words: a rare skin condition characterized by small, scaly, brownish papules that can merge to form larger patches or plaques with a net-like (reticulated) pattern

list.title: Appearance:
list.snippet: Small, scaly, brownish papules that coalesce into larger, reticulated patches.

list.title: Location:
list.snippet: Typically found on the trunk, neck, and upper arms, but can spread to other areas.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Usually asymptomatic, but some individuals may experience mild itching.

list.title: Cause:
list.snippet: The exact cause is unknown, but theories include abnormal keratinization (skin cell growth and shedding), fungal or bacterial involvement, endocrine imbalances, and genetic predisposition.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: Primarily based on clinical appearance and can be confirmed by skin biopsy (showing hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis).

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: Often responds to oral antibiotics like minocycline or doxycycline, although recurrence is common. Topical treatments like retinoids or vitamin D derivatives may also be used.

text_blocks.snippet: Differential diagnosis: It's important to differentiate Gougerot-Carteaud syndrome from tinea versicolor, another skin condition that can appear similar but is caused by a fungal infection.
In summary, Gougerot-Carteaud syndrome is a unique skin condition characterized by its distinctive appearance, potential for recurrence, and variable response to treatment.
